https://www.politico.eu/article/why-peop.text: Hundreds of thousands of Europeans dream of landing one of the European Commission’s coveted civil service jobs, with around 170,000 people applying for just 1,500 entry-level positions at the EU institutions earlier this year. Yet for many who make it inside the EU executive, the reality falls well short of the dream. POLITICO spoke to a dozen officials from different commissioners’ cabinets and Directorates-General, varying in age, nationality and seniority, who described an institution where long hours, cumbersome bureaucracy and, in some cases, toxic management have left them exhausted, alienated and questioning whether the money and prestige are worth it. Advertisement Their experiences varied widely across the Commission’s 30,000-strong workforce — but the same complaints surfaced again and again. Some were granted anonymity to speak frankly about their workplace experiences. “The conditions are more and more difficult,” said Nicolas Mavraganis, president of Union Syndicale Fédérale, an umbrella group linking roughly 20 staff unions across EU and international bodies. A Commission official since 1994, he has led the federation since 2019 and helps steer its representation of member unions in dealings with the institutions. “There is more and more workload, which means more and more pressure.” As Brussels has taken on a more central geopolitical role — responding to Russia’s war against Ukraine, navigating tensions with China and managing an increasingly unpredictable United States — officials said there is a growing sense that every file matters. Few of the complaints POLITICO heard — ranging from stressful projects and difficult bosses to endless bureaucracy and aging offices — are unique to the Commission, and similar stories can be found in ministries, law firms and consultancies across Europe. But officials said the combination of prestige, political pressure and the sheer scale of the institution makes the experience distinctive — and often difficult. “It’s the EU’s executive so people have this weird God complex,” one official said. A Commission spokesperson said the institution was “committed to being a modern, respectful and attractive place to work,” pointing to a review launched by President Ursula von der Leyen into the Commission’s operations. An internal survey found 74 percent of staff rated the Commission an attractive employer, up six percentage points from 2023. Advertisement Comparable public data is scarce. A 2025 staff survey at the European Central Bank found that 85 percent of employees were proud to work there, even as fewer than half considered their workload manageable. The figures point to a broader paradox: loyalty to an institution can remain strong even when day-to-day working conditions frustrate its staff. At the Commission, that gap helps explain why disillusionment does not necessarily lead people to leave. Pressure cooker Openings at the Commission, where employees shape policies affecting more than 450 million Europeans, remain some of the most sought-after public sector jobs. Brussels also remains relatively affordable compared to many Western European capitals, especially on a Commission salary. The financial incentives are considerable too. Successful candidates for AD-5 jobs — the graduate-entry administrator role — earn roughly €6,000 to €7,000 a month before allowances, while Commission officials pay EU tax rather than national income tax, generally resulting in a lighter tax burden and more take-home pay. Family allowances, diplomatic discounts on cars and strong job security only add to the appeal. Some officials POLITICO spoke to even rent an apartment in Brussels while keeping their families in another country, flying home most weekends. But several officials said the prestige of working at the Commission also creates its own pressures. That atmosphere, officials said, filters down into daily life. Every briefing note, policy paper or press release attracts multiple layers of approval. Decisions move through sprawling email chains and successive rounds of revisions, while officials feel pressure to treat even routine work with the urgency of a geopolitical crisis. One official in a commissioner’s cabinet said their days often begin at 7 a.m. or 8 a.m. and end around 7 p.m., with little time away from the office except to accompany their commissioner on missions. Another, working in communications, recalled crying late into the evening because of an overwhelming workload. Advertisement Several officials blamed the bureaucracy itself. Cabinet teams and the Commission’s policy departments, known as Directorates-General, often struggle to communicate effectively, leaving staff chasing approvals and information from one another. “The DGs are waiting for scraps of information from the cabinets, who are so overworked that they don’t have the capacity to provide them that information,” another official working for a commissioner said. “It’s a structural problem. Everyone is trying to get information out of each other.” Another official agreed. “I want to shoot myself sometimes.” The institution’s sheer size can also leave people feeling anonymous. “There are thousands of people at the Commission, so even if you work there for 20 years, most people have never seen you,” a different official not working for a commissioner said. “You’re just this tiny little molecule in this huge organism.” Mixed bag Whether someone enjoys working at the Commission often comes down to luck. First, there’s the boss. Advertisement Officials stressed that experiences can differ dramatically depending on which commissioner you work for. Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra’s cabinet is widely regarded internally as supportive, several officials said, while other commissioners have reputations internally for allowing toxic working cultures to develop, with infighting and power grabs. One senior official in a commissioner’s cabinet has become notorious inside the Berlaymont for “screaming” at staff, according to two officials. An employee at DG ECHO, which coordinates the EU’s humanitarian program, said shouting was routine in their unit. Another former official recalled watching a senior colleague berated over a leaked document in front of other managers. One official said their boss punched them during an argument after work in a bar near the Berlaymont. Several said they felt they had little confidence complaints would be acted upon. The Commission hired a chief confidential counsellor in 2024 to handle harassment complaints and has a team of 40 counsellors across the Commission and executive agencies as part of an “informal” approach to resolving workplace conflict, an official said. Since September 2024, the chief counsellor, who reports to Budget Commissioner Piotr Serafin, has received 960 reports from “colleagues feeling harassed, alleged harassers, witnesses, managers and HR Correspondents,” according to a Commission spokesperson. Advertisement The Commission said 14,000 staff have attended presentations on anti-harassment policy while 2,400 managers have attended mandatory training sessions in the last two years. This increased awareness about how to seek support in dealing with harassment has “generated a relatively high number” of reports to the chief confidential counsellor, the spokesperson said. The chief counsellor, however, “has no mandate to investigate and is not entitled legally to qualify the conduct as harassment as defined in the Staff Regulations,” the spokesperson explained. To make a formal complaint, staff have to go to the Investigation and Disciplinary Office (IDOC) or to the European Anti-Fraud Office (OLAF). The Commission receives around 20 to 25 of those per year, a spokesperson said. Aging offices Then there’s the building. While the Berlaymont has benefited from extensive renovation, other Commission offices are showing their age. During June’s heatwave, staff at the DG AGRI building complained they were working without adequate air conditioning, according to internal communications seen by POLITICO. At DG COMP’s headquarters in Madou Tower, meanwhile, officials were advised not to drink from certain water fountains because of possible contamination, while heating and sanitation systems were “not functioning to the level we should expect,” the acting director-general acknowledged in an email seen by POLITICO. At the Berlaymont, staff on lower levels were left fuming after air conditioning was switched off in the middle of a heat wave but kept on for floors eight and above, which house commissioners and senior officials. An official told POLITICO at the time it was reminiscent of feudalism. Advertisement Experiences varied sharply across the institution, but many officials described the same tension: they remained drawn to the substance of their roles, even as their working conditions proved more frustrating and draining than expected. Over cold pasta in a Commission cafeteria, one official was asked whether they were happy. They shrugged. “It’s interesting work.” For many inside the Commission, that is reason enough to stay. https://www.politico.eu/article/renew-me.text: PARIS — European lawmakers from the Renew parliamentary group will meet President Emmanuel Macron in Paris on Wednesday to discuss how to safeguard the political center he helped build, according to a party official and a government official. The French leader will welcome Renew MEPs to the Elysée Palace in the aftermath of the Alternative for Germany party’s historic victory in Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday . Renew confirmed the meeting on its website , saying lawmakers are meeting with Macron “for an exchange of views on the key European and global issues on the agenda.” Advertisement Advertisement A Renew official, granted anonymity to speak candidly about the meeting agenda, said lawmakers are growing particularly concerned about the prospect of far-right parties taking power in Germany and France, where Marine Le Pen has a commanding lead in the polls for the spring 2027 presidential race. “Pro-Europeans … are worried about what happens after Macron because they recognize his vision and ambition for Europe,” said the official. The burning question on everyone’s lips is what Macron, who cannot run for a third consecutive term, can and will do next. The 48-year-old has given little indication of his plans after he steps down in May 2027, but he has hinted at once again running for the presidency when he is eligible in 2032 . “Lawmakers will question the president on his political future, many would like to see him play a role at a European level,” said the Renew official. But Macron has also indicated that he will focus on his role as French president until the very last day, raising fears he is not preparing the future of his centrist movement when he leaves office. Last May, he said he would “think about what comes next” after the end of his mandate. The talks in Paris will also focus on the upcoming State of the Union speech by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, the Multiannual Financial Framework, social media bans, European preference measures and Ukraine. CORRECTION: This story was updated on Sept. 7 to reflect that Wednesday will not be the first visit to the Elysée for Renew’s MEPs. Advertisement Advertisement

Most Viewed Day Week Hajj Conference Marks Major Leap, More Than Fivefold Growth https://english.aawsat.com/gulf/5340603-hajj-conference-marks-major-leap-more-fivefold-growth Gulf Hajj Conference Marks Major Leap, More Than Fivefold Growth Saudi Minister of Hajj and Umrah meets with journalists on the sidelines of the conference (Asharq Al-Awsat) Jeddah: Asma al Ghabri 18:24-12 November 2026 AD ـ 02 Jumada Al-Alkhirah 1448 AH T T Jeddah: Asma al Ghabri 18:24-12 November 2026 AD ـ 02 Jumada Al-Alkhirah 1448 AH T T Hajj Conference Marks Major Leap, More Than Fivefold Growth Saudi Minister of Hajj and Umrah meets with journalists on the sidelines of the conference (Asharq Al-Awsat) The sixth Hajj Conference and Exhibition wrapped up in the Saudi city of Jeddah on Wednesday, drawing more than 200,000 attendees and participants from over 150 countries, a sharp rise from around 14,000 at its 2022 debut. The four-day gathering brought together officials, experts and service providers for talks and agreements aimed at improving pilgrim services and accelerating preparations for future Hajj seasons. Saudi Minister of Hajj and Umrah Tawfiq Al-Rabiah hailed the event as a "major qualitative leap," citing soaring attendance, wider international participation and a growing number of contracts to improve services for pilgrims. Speaking to reporters at the close of the conference, Al-Rabiah said the event had expanded significantly since its launch in 2022 with just 84 participating companies. The minister said the gathering attracted representatives from more than 150 countries, including ministers, religious leaders, muftis and government officials, reflecting its growing role in shaping pilgrim services. He said the conference had grown more than fivefold, praising the organizers and expressing hope for further improvements in services. Held under the theme "From Makkah to the World" at Jeddah Superdome, the conference was organized by the Ministry of Hajj and Umrah in cooperation with the Pilgrim Experience Program. It brought together government planning and operations agencies, Hajj affairs offices, service providers and technology companies to tackle challenges facing pilgrims and finalize preparations for the 1448 AH Hajj season. The program focused on three areas: infrastructure and operational services; empowerment and integration; and development and sustainability. Discussions covered transportation, accommodation, catering, crowd management, healthcare, security and safety, digital transformation and workforce training. A key focus was the shift toward all-inclusive service packages for pilgrims, alongside tighter contracting procedures, stronger oversight and better ways to measure service quality. Artificial intelligence and data analytics also featured prominently in discussions on streamlining operations and improving the pilgrimage experience. Conference sessions revealed that the Nusuk app had surpassed 65 million users worldwide and offered more than 100 services. The electronic Hajj platform, meanwhile, connects more than 70 entities inside and outside Saudi Arabia, helping coordinate pilgrim reception, transportation, accommodation, group movements and departures. Participants also examined advances in housing, transportation and healthcare, including the growing use of smart technologies, sensors and communications systems. Discussions highlighted stronger governance and oversight, and a shift from measuring operational readiness to assessing how services actually affect pilgrims. On the final day, attention turned to preparations for the next Hajj season, with sessions exploring artificial intelligence, the future of digital services, smart infrastructure, medical readiness and the role of regulations in improving hospitality standards. The contributions of Saudi Scouts to pilgrim services were also highlighted. Specialized workshops on the fourth day addressed emergency response coordination, the shift from prevention to healthcare, food safety, catering and services linked to the Nusuk Card. Other sessions focused on crowd management at the holy sites, early warning systems and improving the skills of Hajj sector workers. Beyond the formal conference sessions, the program featured the Hajj Council, showcasing personal and professional experiences in serving pilgrims, alongside the Innovation Council, the Awareness and Training Diwaniya and the Hajj Affairs Offices Forum. Dedicated spaces also allowed participating organizations to exchange expertise and explore cooperation. The accompanying exhibition showcased technological and operational solutions for the pilgrimage journey, with specialized areas covering healthcare, aviation, technology, innovation and media. A business center and partner platform provided opportunities for meetings, contract negotiations and partnerships ahead of future Hajj seasons. The conference's previous five editions generated more than 1,850 agreements related to pilgrim services and hosted over 310 discussion sessions, underscoring the event's expansion over the years. With the sixth edition concluded, the focus now shifts from discussions and agreements to implementation, as Saudi Arabia seeks to turn new partnerships and technological solutions into practical improvements for the 1448 AH Hajj season. The effort reflects a broader push to strengthen coordination among service providers, improve efficiency and deliver a better experience for pilgrims at every stage of their journey. Saudi Arabia, Kenya Sign Technical Annex to Regulate Domestic Worker Recruitment https://english.aawsat.com/gulf/5340540-saudi-arabia-kenya-sign-technical-annex-regulate-domestic-worker-recruitment Gulf Saudi Arabia, Kenya Sign Technical Annex to Regulate Domestic Worker Recruitment Asharq Al Awsat 15:47-12 November 2026 AD ـ 02 Jumada Al-Alkhirah 1448 AH T T Asharq Al Awsat 15:47-12 November 2026 AD ـ 02 Jumada Al-Alkhirah 1448 AH T T Saudi Arabia, Kenya Sign Technical Annex to Regulate Domestic Worker Recruitment Saudi Vice Minister of Human Resources and Social Development for Labor Abdullah Nasser Abuthnain met with Kenya’s Cabinet Secretary for Labor and Social Protection Alfred Nganga Mutua on Thursday at the ministry’s headquarters in Riyadh, in the presence of the accompanying Kenyan delegation and several senior ministry officials. The meeting discussed ways to strengthen cooperation between Saudi Arabia and Kenya in areas of mutual interest in the labor sector, particularly by developing cooperation mechanisms for the recruitment of domestic workers, improving the effectiveness of pre-departure training and qualification programs, and raising awareness of contractual rights and obligations, SPA reported. These efforts aim to enhance the readiness of domestic workers, improve the quality of recruitment services, promote stability in contractual relations, and protect the rights of all parties. The two sides also discussed mechanisms for strengthening technical coordination, exchanging expertise and best practices in training and qualification, and improving procedures related to the recruitment of domestic workers. These measures aim to enhance the efficiency of recruitment processes, improve their outcomes, and serve the mutual interests of both countries. According to SPA, following the meeting, the Saudi vice minister and Kenya’s cabinet secretary signed a technical annex to the agreement on the recruitment of domestic workers between Saudi Arabia and Kenya, signed on July 5, 2026. The annex is part of efforts to strengthen cooperation and develop the technical and regulatory mechanisms governing the recruitment of domestic workers. The technical annex aims to streamline procedures and reduce the costs of recruiting domestic workers from Kenya to Saudi Arabia. It also seeks to improve the efficiency of recruitment mechanisms, ensure compliance with approved regulations, protect the rights of employers and domestic workers, and regulate the contractual relationship between the two parties. The signing of the annex builds on the longstanding relations and ongoing cooperation between Saudi Arabia and Kenya, reflecting both sides’ commitment to developing their partnership in labor-related fields, improving the efficiency of the recruitment system, and promoting sustainable cooperation that serves the mutual interests of both countries.
